steps: Check codes, location & uncrate

Check local code, permits and inspection; a WETT (Canada) or HEARTH (U.S.A.) certified installer is strongly recommended. Confirm the floor carries approx. 500lbs (227Kg) plus venting, then remove the wood top, supports and the two pallet screws.

Never install in a makeshift or temporary manner. Don't connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance. In a manufactured or mobile home, don't install in a sleeping room. The fireplace may not be installed in a factory built fireplace unless tested with the fireplace.

Location

Allow room in front for ember protection and clearances. Ideally the chimney passes through without cutting floor or roof joists, penetrates the highest part of the roof, stays clear of roof offsets, trees and obstructions, and has the fewest offsets possible. The unit may sit directly on a combustible floor or on a raised base.

Weight of the fireplace system (floor check)approx. 500lbs (227Kg), plus the venting
Maker's website: Weight 480 lb.

Mobile homes

  • U.S.A.: install per HUD "Manufactured Home Construction and Safety".
  • Canada: provide access openings into the chase for inspection, with covers that need a household tool to open.
Frame the chase
Frame to the minimums in Figure 7, adjusted for drywall (drywall counts as combustible). Keep at least 6' (1.83m) from the base of the unit to the ceiling inside the chase.

• Top front framing as in Figure 8, with no wood framing directly in front of the chimney system.
  • The fireplace must not contact insulation or loose fill. If you insulate the chase, cover it with drywall or non-combustible panels; don't insulate the front portion of the chase above the unit.
  • The open volume inside the chase is required for heat management: no recess, shelves or cupboards above the fireplace.

The wall and corner framing minimums are given only as a dimensioned drawing (Figure 7); read them from the page. The rating label gives the framing opening as 42 in. / 1.07m.
Framing kit & set the unit

Assemble the steel framing kit (legs to the bottom stud, center supports, then the top stud). Push the fireplace in flush with the front framing, set the kit on top legs-down and flush, and fasten it to the chase framing.

The kit holds TEKS screws (#8 x 1/2"), top/bottom studs (41-3/4"), center support studs (15") and framing kit legs (3-1/2"). Secure the unit if local code requires. The kit gives a flat surface for the outer non-combustible board, so keep its front edge flush with the fireplace and the chase framing.
Install the chimney

Listed 6" chimney (UL 103HT in the U.S., CAN-ULC S629 in Canada) with its outlet 15' to 35' above the base of the unit. Chimney maker's anchor plate in the flue collar, a firestop at every floor, 2" to combustibles.

1. Plumb from the flue collar; cut and frame square holes in each floor, ceiling and roof; mount firestops and radiation shields. A radiation shield/firestop is required for each floor/wall the chimney passes through.
  2. Keep 2"(51mm) between chimney and combustibles and don't fill the space with insulation. Fit insulation shields as code requires.
  3. Insert the chimney maker's fireplace anchor plate into the flue collar, seal the joint with stove cement and secure with stainless steel screws. Plates that don't sit flush (some brands, including ICC) need spacer Part #11220002; make sure the plate fully engages the flue collar.
  4. Rest the chimney on the anchor plate and run it through the roof; no joints between ceiling and roof; secure each connection with three #8x½" stainless screws.
  5. Fit the roof radiation shield, flashing and storm collar per the vent maker, keeping the vapour barrier sealed. Use roof braces if the chimney extends more than 5'(1.5m) above the roof.
  6. Attach the rain cap and check the flashing for leaks.

Offsets: max four 30° elbows (U.S.A.) or four 45° elbows (Canada); minimum 36" of chimney before the first elbow (Figure 12); support after the first 20'(6.1m). Masonry: see the Chimney spec and Figure 13.
Combustion air

Outside air: 4" rigid or flex pipe from the side or rear adapter to an approved 4" inlet vent cap with rodent screen, at least 5ft (1.5m) below the chimney outlet. Or draw room air through the surround or chase floor ducts.

• Outside air must come from outdoors, finished with an approved vent hood, and the fireplace must be secured to the structure so the duct can't dislodge.
  • The adapter ships inside the fireplace in the hardware kit; fit it on either side and move the cover plate to the opposite side as needed. Insulated flex is recommended in cold climates.
  • Cut the hole in the closest exterior wall or in the floor inside the chase, cover it with min. 20GA wire mesh rodent screen, and provide water protection as code requires.
  • Never terminate in an attic space or garage.

Consult local code or CAN/CSA-B365 before proceeding.
Wire the blowers

Bring 120 VAC (Romex 14/2 or equivalent) through the strain relief into the junction box on the right side of the support base, via a wall switch or fan speed controller (not supplied). Rating 115 V, 60 Hz, 1.1A.
Connect per the wiring diagram (Figure 17). All connections by a certified/licensed electrician, to local code, or CSA C22.2 in Canada and ANSI/NFPA 70 in the U.S.A.
Ember protection & safety strip
Fit a 2" deep metal safety strip the width of the unit, half under the fireplace front. Ember protection extends 18" in front and 8" each side of the door: UL1618 Type 1, min. 20GA steel equivalent.

Tile, brick, slate, stone or metal meeting UL1618 Type 1; non-combustible, minimum K value 23.7 btu/ft h ˚F. Seal the space between the fireplace and the hearth extension with non-combustible material such as sand-cement grout. For a raised unit, a 2" x 2" angled piece can be used against the non-combustible face. U.S. and Canadian layouts are drawn separately (Figures 19 and 20).
Cement board & facing edge

Cover the front with non-combustible cement board from the floor to 6ft. (1.83m) above the bottom of the fireplace (or 43 1/2" from the top facing stop), 44" wide, centred. Nothing inside the facing edge/stop.

Fasten and finish joints per the board maker. Board or finishing material inside the built-in facing edge/stop causes improper panel fit and overheating of the fireplace and blowers, and may not be covered under warranty. Figure 21 also marks a 30in2 (194cm2) chase air inlet, which can sit in various locations, including the other side of the chase.
Facing, mantel & front trim

Non-combustible facing only within 12" of the outer door edge, under the door to the floor, and above the air deflector up to the mantel chart height. Hook the front trim into the bracket slots, push in and slide down.

Mantel height from the base of the unit runs from 46 1/2" for a 4" deep mantel to 50 1/2" for 12" deep (see the Mantel card). Mantel side facing (max 4" deep): 12" from the side of the door. The backing plate is factory-installed; a replacement fastens to the casing-side brackets with four screws.
Install the firebrick

With the heater upright: rear bricks two each side of the baffle tube, then the vertical side bricks with the horizontal side brick tucked under the retaining tabs, then four on the floor. 14 full-size bricks, 9" X 4 1/2" X 1 1/4".

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
You light this fireplace by hand. The air control lever sits under the ash shelf: all the way to the left is High, the other stop is Low.

  1. Slide the air control all the way left, to High.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the center and crisscross several pieces of small, dry kindling over it. Light the paper and leave the door open about 1" to 4" until the kindling is fully in flame.
  3. When the kindling has burned down by half, add 2-3 small split pieces or small logs about 1" in diameter. Keep the door cracked about 1" to 2" until they're fully lit.
  4. When that has burned down by half and you have a good bed of coals, add your regular wood and close the door.

If the new load is slow to catch, crack the door 1" to 2" and close it as soon as the wood lights. If the flames falter or go out, crack it again until the wood relights.

Never leave the fireplace unattended with the door open, and never use gasoline, lighter fluid or similar liquids to start a fire.

Your first 2-3 fires

The paint cures at operating temperature and gives off smoke and fumes. Open windows and doors. Small children, older people and anyone with breathing problems should leave the area during this hot burn. Smoke detectors may go off; don't disconnect them.

burn.title: Air control & reloading
burn.html:
The air control sets your heat: move it between the High and Low stops. Every home is different, so find your setting by trial and error and note it for next time.

Smoke pouring down the glass (a "waterfall") means you turned the air down before the fire was fully going after loading, or went too low too quickly.

Adding wood

  1. Slide the air control to High (all the way left) and give the fire time to brighten.
  2. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't puff back and flames don't roll out.
  3. Load dry wood of mixed shapes and sizes, about 16" long, with room for air between pieces. Keep the load no higher than 7" from the firebox floor.

Overnight and restarting

For long burns, use unsplit logs and char them completely on High before turning the air to Low. To restart, rake the hot embers toward the front, add a couple of dry split logs, close the door and set the air to High. Once the wood has charred, reset the air.

Use High only for start-up or a fresh load, not for long periods. The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory; altering it is against federal regulations.

wood.title: Choosing and testing your wood
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood burns more efficiently and cleaner than softwood or green wood. Season wood for six months or more and store it under cover, away from flame and heat.

Wet or green wood smoulders, makes lots of smoke and creosote, gives little heat and tends to go out.

Test a piece

Put a large piece on a good bed of coals:

  • Dry: it's burning on more than one side within one minute.
  • Damp: it turns black and lights within three minutes.
  • Soaked: it sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes. Don't burn it.

Never burn

Wet, green or unseasoned wood, salt-water wood, treated wood, railroad ties, plywood, particleboard, garbage, paper products or cardboard, coal or charcoal, materials containing plastic, rubber (including tires) or asbestos, lawn clippings and yard waste, construction or demolition debris, manure or animal remains, solvents, waste petroleum products, paints, paint thinners or asphalt products. Burning any of these may release toxic fumes, or make the heater ineffective and cause smoke. Salt-water wood and garbage contain chlorides that rapidly destroy metal and void the warranty. Paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax fire starters are fine for lighting.

Charcoal and other fuels can make large amounts of carbon monoxide, a gas you can't smell or taste that can kill. Never barbecue in the fireplace.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Clean the glass with fireplace glass cleaner, and only when the fireplace is cold.

  • Never scrape it with anything that could scratch.
  • Don't use abrasive cleaners.
  • Don't clean it while it's hot.

What the deposit tells you

A light brown, dusty film that wipes off easily usually means good combustion and dry wood, so your chimney is probably fairly clean too. A black, greasy deposit that's hard to remove comes from wet or green wood and burning too slowly, and the same heavy buildup is forming in your chimney.

If it keeps getting dirty, the usual causes are wet wood, turning the air down before there's a good bed of coals and the wood is charred, low draft, or a leaking door gasket.

Don't slam the door or let logs stick out where they can hit the glass. Cracked or broken glass must be replaced before you use the fireplace again, with ceramic glass from your dealer, never another material.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Remove ashes often: embers can roll out the door and start a fire. Keep an ash base of 1" to 4".

  • Take ashes out only when the fire has burned down and both the ashes and the fireplace are cold.
  • When ashes are 3 to 4 inches deep, remove the excess. Leave about 1" on the firebox floor to help keep a hot bed of coals for the next fire.
  • Keep the front of the firebox clear. That's where boost air comes in, and ash buildup there blocks it.

Storing and disposing

Put ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn. If you'll bury or scatter them, keep them in the closed container until all cinders are thoroughly cool. Don't put other waste in it.

chimney.title: Creosote and chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow fires give off tar and vapours that condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot.

  • Inspect and clean the chimney before your first fire each season, and have the chimney and connector inspected at least once every two months while you're burning. Check daily for creosote until you know how often you need to clean.
  • Remove creosote once it reaches 3 mm or more.
  • Burn dry wood with plenty of air: small loads, with the air control fairly wide open for the first 10 to 30 minutes after each loading.

Signs of a chimney fire

Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney, a roaring sound, or the chimney vibrating.

If it happens

  1. Get everyone ready to leave, with an agreed meeting place outside.
  2. Close the air inlet with the air control.
  3. Call the fire department. Keep a fire extinguisher handy.
  4. Before the next fire, have the chimney cleaned and checked for stress and cracks, and check the combustibles around the chimney and roof.

Pacific Energy strongly recommends inspection by a certified chimney professional.

trouble.title: Over-firing and draft
trouble.html:
Don't over-fire. Pushing the fireplace past its design output can permanently damage it and the chimney, shortens its life, and may void the warranty.

What causes over-firing

  • Burning with the door open
  • Damaged door gaskets letting in extra air
  • Kiln-dried lumber, mill ends or paper waste
  • Long or constant burning on High

Draft

Too much: a burn you can't control, or a fireplace part or the chimney glowing red. Too little: smoke puffing back into the room, or smoke leaking from the fireplace and chimney joints.

Quick checks

  • Low heat: wet wood, a fire that's too small, or a plugged chimney.
  • Won't burn overnight: air set too high, not enough wood (unsplit logs work best), or too much draft.
  • Won't burn at all: blocked combustion air, or a plugged, oversized or unsuitable chimney. Call your dealer.

care.title: Routine checks & care
care.html:
Check these parts for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections and excessive warping:

WeeklyFirebrick (cracks) · door gasket (sagging, placement, damage)
MonthlyBrick rails and tabs · air riser tube at the back · back of the airwash chamber · baffle locking pin · boost manifold cover
When the chimney is cleanedBaffle, baffle board/blanket and gasket · top heat shield and bolt · brick rails · manifold

Door gasket and baffle

The 7/8" fiberglass rope gasket needs only light pressure to seal; inspect it now and then and replace it if needed. Some baffle warping, up to 1/4", is normal. More than that, or any cracking or breakage, means replacement: contact your dealer. Running with broken parts can damage other parts and may void your warranty.

Blowers

At least once a year, lift the front trim up and pull it away. The blowers sit on each side of the firebox; gently vacuum dust from their intakes and wheels.

Burn directly on the firebricks, never on a grate or andirons, and replace broken or missing bricks.

safety.title: Safety around the fireplace
safety.html:
• Hot glass will cause burns. Don't touch it until it has cooled, and never let children touch it. Keep children, clothing and furniture away while it's burning.
  • Keep the door closed while burning and open it only to add wood. An open door lets sparks out and can pull too much air from the room, possibly causing suffocation.
  • Keep combustible materials in the room 48" away, and don't store wood within the installation clearances, including in front of the fireplace.
  • Never use gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire, and keep them well away.
  • Don't alter the combustion air control assembly. It's hazardous and voids the warranty.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors may be required near the fireplace. Pacific Energy strongly recommends them either way.
In extreme cold, especially with very slow fires, the top of an exposed chimney can ice up and partly block it, letting flue gases into the house. Anything that causes negative pressure in the home can also pull fumes inside.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Pacific Energy's Wood Products Warranty covers the original registered purchaser.

Limited lifetime (10 years)Parts only: porcelain finish, glass (thermal breakage, not impact), plating, firebox and baffle
3 year comprehensiveParts and labor on any defective part, including blowers, speed controls and thermal switches

Not covered

  • Labor under the lifetime coverage
  • Firebox rails and heat shields (excluded from the lifetime warranty)
  • Firebrick, gaskets and ceramic fiber blankets
  • Misuse, abuse, improper installation, accident, lack of maintenance or modification

Excessive draft, heating too large an area, or contaminated fuel (high sodium, plastics, chemicals) may void it.

Making a claim

Report the problem to your Pacific Energy dealer with proof of purchase, the purchase date, and the model name and serial number. The serial number is on the product certification label or the cover of your installation manual. Register your fireplace at pacificenergy.net/register.

review.notes: One manual and one rating label cover both catalog models (manual writes the Arch as 'FP16 AR LE' / 'FP16AR LE'). All ratings, clearances and install steps are given once; the only model split is the p. 31 parts list (door casting, door assembly, front trim), shown per model in specDoor. Items 10/12/19 are read as the FP16 LE parts because the arch versions (21/23/24) are named 'Arch'; the list never names the FP16 LE itself. The p. 32 diagram callouts 25 and 26 (and item 22) have no entry in the parts list. 'Peak BTU/Hr Output' on p. 3 is printed with no value and its footnote 4 is missing, so the website's Heat Output (Cord Wood) 70,000 BTU has no manual counterpart; it is shown as a Maker's website note after the EPA output in specOutput and listed in catalog_mismatches. Not stated in the manual: heating area, firebox volume ('NEO 1.6' appears only in part names), view/glass area, blower cfm, non-catalytic. Figure-only dimensions not transcribed: overall dimensions (p. 15 Figure 6), framing minimums (p. 16 Figure 7), US vs Canada ember-protector layouts incl. 34"/50" (p. 23 Figures 19-20), masonry callouts (p. 20 Figure 13), a 1 1/2" callout on p. 24. Self-labelled figure callouts used: 'Minimum 36" length of Chimney before first elbow' (p. 19), '30in2 (194cm2) chase air inlet' (p. 24), 33" top of unit to ceiling (p. 18, also label E on p. 3). Metric equivalents vary between pages (18" = 457/455/460 mm; 8" = 203/200 mm; 33" = 838/835 mm; 12" facing = 292mm in p. 27 text vs 305mm in its figure; lighting step 3 on p. 7 prints 2"(100mm)); the guide uses the inch values, which agree. Framing kit quantities on p. 17 are garbled and omitted. p. 3 French label text names an optional heat distribution duct kit (WODC.RHKA) that appears only in French; not used. Lighting is fully manual (no ignition system). No error-code table; faults are from the p. 30 troubleshooting chart.
